title: Consistent Hashing: why modulo hashing fails at scale

meta.yt_title: Why Modulo Hashing Fails at Scale (Consistent Hashing Explained) #shorts
meta.yt_description:
Why simple hash(key) % N breaks distributed databases at scale, and how consistent hashing solves it.

• Modulo hashing reshuffles almost every key when adding or removing a server
• Consistent hashing maps servers and keys onto a 2^32 circular ring
• Requests route clockwise to the nearest server node
• Adding a new server only moves 1/N of keys, eliminating cache stampedes

Voiceover is AI-generated. Source: Karger et al. (MIT Consistent Hashing), Amazon Dynamo Paper.
meta.ig_caption:
Why does `hash(key) % N` fail at scale? 🤯

If you have 4 cache servers and add a 5th, normal modulo hashing invalidates 80% of your cached data overnight.

⚡ Consistent Hashing maps both keys and servers to a 360° hash ring (0 to 2³² - 1)
🔄 Keys walk clockwise to the nearest server
🛡️ Adding a server only moves 1/N of the keys

This is how Discord, Cassandra, and Amazon Dynamo scale without downtime.

Follow @stackshade for more.

Voiceover is AI-generated. Source: MIT Consistent Hashing paper, Amazon Dynamo.

scenes.say: Most engineers route cache keys using hash of key modulo N. But adding one server invalidates almost everything.

els.text: Change N from 4 to 5 → almost every key moves

scenes.say: Consistent hashing fixes this. Both servers and keys are hashed onto a circular ring from zero to two to the thirty second.

els.text: Servers and keys share the same 2^32 address space

children.text:
KEYS ROUTE CLOCKWISE
**TO FIRST NEAREST SERVER**

scenes.say: When a new server joins, it only takes a tiny slice from its neighbor. Only one divided by N keys move.

els.text: How Discord, Cassandra, and DynamoDB scale seamlessly.
